books.title: Chemistry Part I
books.edition: Reprint 2026-27 (first edition March 2006; revised edition October 2022; reprinted March 2024, June 2024, January 2025 and February 2026)

books.title: Chemistry Part II
books.edition: Reprint 2026-27 (first edition March 2006; revised edition October 2022; reprinted March 2024, June 2024, January 2025 and February 2026)

source.method: unit titles from each book's Contents page; topics from each unit PDF's numbered section and subsection headings, and in Thermodynamics and Classification of Elements from the lettered sub-headings the book uses inside a section (General Introduction is not a topic; a parent heading that is only a short lead-in to its subsections is not a separate topic; very short adjacent subsections are joined under one title naming them; where several sections share a heading such as 'Preparation', the topic title adds the compound class)

topics.title: Importance of Chemistry
objectives: Student can describe the role of chemistry in areas such as medicines, fertilisers, materials and the environment
Student can describe the development of chemistry in ancient India, known as Rasayan Shastra
visualIdeas: a collage of medicines, fertilisers, alloys and plastics linked to chemistry

topics.title: States of Matter
objectives: Student can compare the arrangement and movement of particles in solids, liquids and gases
Student can explain why solids have definite shape and volume, liquids have definite volume, and gases have neither
visualIdeas: particles packed in a solid, close but mobile in a liquid, far apart in a gas

topics.title: Classification of Matter
objectives: Student can classify matter into mixtures and pure substances, and mixtures into homogeneous and heterogeneous
Student can classify pure substances into elements and compounds and give examples of each
visualIdeas: a tree chart: matter, mixtures and pure substances, elements and compounds
atoms and molecules of an element and of a compound

topics.title: Physical and Chemical Properties
objectives: Student can distinguish physical properties, measured without changing a substance's identity, from chemical properties that need a chemical change
Student can give examples such as colour, odour, melting point and density versus composition, combustibility and reactivity with acids and bases
visualIdeas: a table sorting properties of a substance into physical and chemical

topics.title: Measurement of Physical Properties and the International System of Units (SI)
objectives: Student can explain that a measurement needs a number and a unit, and name the metric system as the basis of SI
Student can list the seven SI base quantities and units and use SI prefixes for multiples and submultiples
visualIdeas: a table of SI base units beside prefixes from pico to tera

topics.title: Mass, Weight, Volume, Density and Temperature
objectives: Student can distinguish mass from weight and use units and devices for measuring volume
Student can calculate density as mass per unit volume
Student can convert between the Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin temperature scales
visualIdeas: an analytical balance and volumetric glassware
three thermometers side by side in degrees C, degrees F and K

topics.title: Scientific Notation
objectives: Student can write very large and very small numbers in the form N x 10^n
Student can multiply, divide, add and subtract numbers written in scientific notation

topics.title: Significant Figures
objectives: Student can distinguish precision (closeness of repeated measurements) from accuracy (agreement with the true value)
Student can count significant figures using the rules for zeros and exact numbers
Student can apply the rules for significant figures in addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, and round off results
visualIdeas: a target board showing precise-but-inaccurate and precise-and-accurate shots

topics.title: Dimensional Analysis
objectives: Student can convert units using unit factors such as 1 in = 2.54 cm
Student can carry units through a calculation like algebraic quantities
visualIdeas: a chain of unit factors converting days to seconds

topics.title: Law of Conservation of Mass, Definite Proportions and Multiple Proportions
objectives: Student can state the law of conservation of mass given by Lavoisier
Student can state the law of definite proportions with an example of a compound from different sources
Student can state the law of multiple proportions and check it with the masses of oxygen combining with a fixed mass of hydrogen in water and hydrogen peroxide
visualIdeas: two samples of copper carbonate with identical percentage composition

topics.title: Gay Lussac's Law of Gaseous Volumes and Avogadro's Law
objectives: Student can state Gay Lussac's law that reacting gases combine in simple whole-number ratios by volume
Student can state Avogadro's law that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules
visualIdeas: two volumes of hydrogen and one volume of oxygen giving two volumes of water vapour

topics.title: Dalton's Atomic Theory
objectives: Student can state the postulates of Dalton's atomic theory
Student can explain how the theory accounts for the laws of chemical combination and name what it could not explain
visualIdeas: atoms as solid spheres combining in fixed ratios

topics.title: Atomic Mass and Average Atomic Mass
objectives: Student can define the atomic mass unit as one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom
Student can calculate the average atomic mass of an element from the masses and natural abundances of its isotopes
visualIdeas: isotopes of carbon with their percentage abundances

topics.title: Molecular Mass and Formula Mass
objectives: Student can calculate the molecular mass of a substance as the sum of atomic masses of its atoms
Student can use formula mass for ionic compounds such as sodium chloride that have no discrete molecules
visualIdeas: a glucose formula with atomic masses added up
the packing of Na+ and Cl- ions in sodium chloride

topics.title: Mole Concept and Molar Masses
objectives: Student can define one mole as 6.022 x 10^23 entities (Avogadro constant)
Student can relate the molar mass in grams to the atomic or molecular mass and convert between mass, moles and number of particles
visualIdeas: one mole each of water, sodium chloride and sugar on a bench

topics.title: Percentage Composition
objectives: Student can calculate the mass per cent of each element in a compound from its formula
Student can explain why percentage composition is used to check the purity of a sample
visualIdeas: a pie chart of the mass per cent of elements in ethanol

topics.title: Empirical Formula for Molecular Formula
objectives: Student can distinguish an empirical formula from a molecular formula
Student can find the empirical formula from percentage composition and the molecular formula from the molar mass
visualIdeas: a step table: mass per cent, moles, simplest ratio, empirical formula

topics.title: Stoichiometry and Stoichiometric Calculations
objectives: Student can explain what a balanced chemical equation tells us about moles, masses and volumes of reactants and products
Student can balance a chemical equation and use it to calculate amounts of reactants and products
visualIdeas: the combustion of methane with mole, mass and volume ratios under each species

topics.title: Limiting Reagent
objectives: Student can identify the limiting reagent as the reactant used up first, which limits the amount of product
Student can calculate the amount of product formed when reactants are not in stoichiometric proportion
visualIdeas: sandwich-making analogy with more bread than filling
reactant particles with some left over after reaction

topics.title: Reactions in Solutions
objectives: Student can express the concentration of a solution as mass per cent, mole fraction, molarity and molality
Student can calculate molarity and molality of a solution and explain why molality does not change with temperature
visualIdeas: a volumetric flask filled to the mark for a 1 M solution

topics.title: Discovery of Electron
objectives: Student can describe cathode ray discharge tube experiments and the properties of cathode rays
Student can explain why cathode rays were identified as negatively charged particles called electrons
visualIdeas: a cathode ray tube with a beam travelling from cathode to anode

topics.title: Charge to Mass Ratio of Electron
objectives: Student can describe how Thomson measured e/m of the electron using deflection in electric and magnetic fields
Student can state that the deflection depends on the charge, the mass and the field strengths
visualIdeas: a cathode ray beam bent by electric plates and a magnet

topics.title: Charge on the Electron
objectives: Student can describe Millikan's oil drop experiment for measuring the charge on the electron
Student can calculate the mass of the electron from its charge and e/m ratio
visualIdeas: charged oil drops falling between charged plates viewed through a telescope

topics.title: Discovery of Protons and Neutrons
objectives: Student can describe how canal rays led to the discovery of positively charged protons
Student can describe Chadwick's discovery of the neutron and compare the charge and mass of electron, proton and neutron
visualIdeas: a table of electron, proton and neutron with their charges and masses

topics.title: Thomson Model of Atom
objectives: Student can describe Thomson's model of the atom as a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it
Student can state what the model explained (overall neutrality) and its limitations
visualIdeas: the plum pudding or watermelon picture of an atom

topics.title: Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom
objectives: Student can describe the alpha particle scattering experiment and its observations
Student can state the conclusions: a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus with electrons moving around it
visualIdeas: alpha particles striking gold foil with most passing through and a few bouncing back

topics.title: Atomic Number and Mass Number
objectives: Student can define atomic number as the number of protons and mass number as the number of nucleons
Student can find the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons from the symbol of an atom or ion
visualIdeas: the notation 35/17 Cl with each number labelled

topics.title: Isobars and Isotopes
objectives: Student can define isotopes as atoms with the same atomic number but different mass numbers, and isobars as atoms with the same mass number
Student can explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties
visualIdeas: the three isotopes of hydrogen with their protons and neutrons

topics.title: Drawbacks of Rutherford Model
objectives: Student can explain why an electron in circular orbit should, by classical theory, radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus
Student can state that the Rutherford model says nothing about electron distribution and energies
visualIdeas: an electron spiralling into the nucleus

topics.title: Wave Nature of Electromagnetic Radiation
objectives: Student can describe electromagnetic radiation as oscillating electric and magnetic fields travelling at the speed of light
Student can relate frequency, wavelength and wavenumber, c = nu lambda
Student can describe the electromagnetic spectrum and the visible range
visualIdeas: electric and magnetic field components of a light wave
the electromagnetic spectrum with the visible band expanded

topics.title: Particle Nature of Electromagnetic Radiation: Planck's Quantum Theory
objectives: Student can describe black-body radiation and the photoelectric effect as phenomena that wave theory could not explain
Student can state Planck's quantum theory, E = h nu, and calculate the energy of a photon
Student can explain the photoelectric effect using threshold frequency and the kinetic energy of ejected electrons
visualIdeas: light falling on a metal surface ejecting electrons
intensity-wavelength curves of a black body at different temperatures

topics.title: Evidence for the Quantized Electronic Energy Levels: Atomic Spectra
objectives: Student can distinguish continuous, emission and absorption spectra
Student can describe the line spectrum of hydrogen and its series (Lyman, Balmer, Paschen and others) using the Rydberg formula
visualIdeas: the line spectrum of hydrogen with the Balmer lines in the visible region

topics.title: Bohr's Model for Hydrogen Atom
objectives: Student can state the postulates of Bohr's model: stationary orbits, quantised angular momentum and energy changes by absorbing or emitting radiation
Student can use the expressions for the radius and energy of the nth orbit of hydrogen and hydrogen-like species
visualIdeas: concentric orbits with energy levels getting closer together as n increases

topics.title: Explanation of Line Spectrum of Hydrogen
objectives: Student can explain the lines in the hydrogen spectrum as transitions of the electron between energy levels
Student can calculate the wavelength or frequency of radiation emitted in a given transition
visualIdeas: an energy level diagram with arrows for Lyman, Balmer and Paschen transitions

topics.title: Limitations of Bohr's Model
objectives: Student can list the shortcomings of Bohr's model, such as failing for multi-electron atoms and not explaining fine structure or the Zeeman and Stark effects
Student can state that the model could not explain the ability of atoms to form molecules by bonds
visualIdeas: a spectral line splitting into several lines in a magnetic field

topics.title: Dual Behaviour of Matter
objectives: Student can state de Broglie's relation lambda = h/mv for the wavelength of a moving particle
Student can explain why wave properties are noticeable for electrons but not for everyday objects
visualIdeas: an electron wave fitting around an orbit
a cricket ball and an electron with their de Broglie wavelengths compared

topics.title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
objectives: Student can state that the position and momentum of an electron cannot both be known exactly at the same time
Student can explain the significance of the principle for microscopic objects and why it rules out definite orbits in the Bohr model
visualIdeas: a photon striking an electron and changing its path during measurement

topics.title: Quantum Mechanical Model of Atom
objectives: Student can state that quantum mechanics describes electrons with the Schrodinger equation and wave functions
Student can list the important features of the quantum mechanical model: quantised energy levels, orbitals and probability of finding an electron
visualIdeas: a probability cloud of an electron around the nucleus

topics.title: Orbitals and Quantum Numbers
objectives: Student can describe the principal, azimuthal and magnetic quantum numbers and the values they can take
Student can name subshells as s, p, d, f and work out the number of orbitals in each
Student can describe the electron spin quantum number and its two values
visualIdeas: a table of n, l and m values with the subshells and number of orbitals

topics.title: Shapes of Atomic Orbitals
objectives: Student can describe the shapes of s, p and d orbitals using boundary surface diagrams
Student can find the number of radial and angular nodes of an orbital
visualIdeas: boundary surface diagrams of 1s, 2p and 3d orbitals

topics.title: Energies of Orbitals
objectives: Student can explain that in hydrogen the orbital energy depends only on n, but in multi-electron atoms it depends on n and l
Student can use the (n + l) rule and the idea of shielding to order orbital energies
visualIdeas: energy level diagrams for hydrogen and for a multi-electron atom side by side

topics.title: Filling of Orbitals in Atom
objectives: Student can state the aufbau principle and the order of filling of orbitals
Student can state Pauli's exclusion principle and Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity
visualIdeas: the diagonal arrow chart of the order of filling orbitals
orbital boxes filled one arrow at a time before pairing

topics.title: Electronic Configuration of Atoms
objectives: Student can write the electronic configuration of atoms using spdf notation and orbital diagrams
Student can identify exceptions such as chromium and copper
visualIdeas: orbital box diagrams for carbon, nitrogen and oxygen

topics.title: Stability of Completely Filled and Half Filled Subshells
objectives: Student can explain the extra stability of half-filled and completely filled subshells using symmetrical distribution and exchange energy
Student can use this to explain the configurations of chromium and copper
visualIdeas: possible exchanges of parallel spins in a d5 configuration

chapters.title: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

topics.title: Why do we Need to Classify Elements?
objectives: Student can explain why classifying the many known elements makes their study systematic
Student can describe how the number of known elements grew over time
visualIdeas: a timeline of the number of known elements

topics.title: Genesis of Periodic Classification
objectives: Student can describe Dobereiner's triads and Newlands' law of octaves and their limitations
Student can state Mendeleev's periodic law and explain how he left gaps and predicted properties of eka-aluminium and eka-silicon
visualIdeas: Mendeleev's table with gaps marked for gallium and germanium
Newlands' octaves compared to musical notes

topics.title: Modern Periodic Law and the Present Form of the Periodic Table
objectives: Student can state the modern periodic law based on atomic number, following Moseley's work
Student can describe the long form of the periodic table with 18 groups and 7 periods
visualIdeas: the long form periodic table with groups and periods labelled

topics.title: Nomenclature of Elements with Atomic Numbers > 100
objectives: Student can name elements with atomic number above 100 using the IUPAC numerical roots
Student can write the temporary symbol of an element from its atomic number
visualIdeas: a table of digit roots: nil, un, bi, tri and so on

topics.title: Electronic Configurations of Elements and the Periodic Table
objectives: Student can relate the period number to the principal quantum number of the outermost shell
Student can explain why elements in the same group have similar outer electronic configurations
visualIdeas: the periodic table coloured by the subshell being filled

topics.title: The s-Block Elements
objectives: Student can describe the outer configuration ns1 and ns2 of group 1 and 2 elements
Student can describe s-block elements as reactive metals with low ionization enthalpies that form ionic compounds
visualIdeas: groups 1 and 2 highlighted on the periodic table

topics.title: The p-Block Elements
objectives: Student can describe the outer configuration ns2 np1 to ns2 np6 of groups 13 to 18
Student can describe the noble gases as having closed valence shells and the change from metals to non-metals across the block
visualIdeas: groups 13 to 18 highlighted with the noble gases in a separate colour

topics.title: The d-Block and f-Block Elements
objectives: Student can describe d-block (transition) elements as metals with general configuration (n-1)d1-10 ns0-2, mostly forming coloured ions and showing variable oxidation states
Student can describe f-block (inner transition) elements, the lanthanoids and actinoids, placed separately at the bottom of the table
visualIdeas: the periodic table with the d-block in the centre and the f-block rows below

topics.title: Metals, Non-metals and Metalloids
objectives: Student can describe the general properties of metals and non-metals and where they lie in the periodic table
Student can identify metalloids such as silicon, germanium and arsenic along the zig-zag line
visualIdeas: a zig-zag line separating metals from non-metals with metalloids along it

topics.title: Atomic Radius and Ionic Radius
objectives: Student can explain the trends of atomic radius down a group and across a period in terms of nuclear charge and shells
Student can explain why a cation is smaller and an anion larger than its parent atom, and compare isoelectronic species
visualIdeas: circles of increasing size down group 1 and decreasing across period 2

topics.title: Ionization Enthalpy
objectives: Student can define first and second ionization enthalpy
Student can explain the trends of ionization enthalpy across a period and down a group using shielding and effective nuclear charge
Student can explain anomalies such as boron having a lower first ionization enthalpy than beryllium
visualIdeas: a graph of first ionization enthalpy against atomic number with peaks at the noble gases

topics.title: Electron Gain Enthalpy
objectives: Student can define electron gain enthalpy and explain why it can be negative or positive
Student can describe its general trends in the periodic table and why noble gases have large positive values
visualIdeas: an atom gaining an electron with energy released

topics.title: Electronegativity
objectives: Student can define electronegativity as the ability of an atom in a compound to attract shared electrons
Student can describe its trends and relate it to metallic and non-metallic character, using the Pauling scale
visualIdeas: an electronegativity map of the periodic table

topics.title: Periodic Trends in Chemical Properties
objectives: Student can explain the periodicity of valence or oxidation states from the number of outer electrons
Student can explain the anomalous properties of second period elements, such as lithium and beryllium, using their small size and lack of d orbitals
visualIdeas: formulas of hydrides and oxides across period 3 showing valence

topics.title: Periodic Trends and Chemical Reactivity
objectives: Student can relate reactivity to ionization enthalpy and electron gain enthalpy at the two ends of a period
Student can explain why oxides on the left are basic, on the right acidic, and in the centre amphoteric or neutral
visualIdeas: oxides across period 3 labelled basic, amphoteric and acidic

topics.title: Kössel-Lewis Approach to Chemical Bonding
objectives: Student can write Lewis symbols showing the valence electrons of an atom
Student can state the octet rule and explain the formation of ionic bonds by electron transfer in Kössel's approach
visualIdeas: Lewis symbols of the second period elements
Na giving an electron to Cl to form Na+ and Cl-

topics.title: Covalent Bond
objectives: Student can describe a covalent bond as a shared pair of electrons, as proposed by Langmuir and Lewis
Student can show single, double and triple bonds in molecules such as Cl2, O2 and N2
visualIdeas: two chlorine atoms sharing a pair of electrons

topics.title: Lewis Representation of Simple Molecules (the Lewis Structures)
objectives: Student can draw Lewis structures by counting valence electrons, choosing the central atom and completing octets
Student can draw Lewis structures for molecules and ions such as CO, NO2- and CO3 2-
visualIdeas: step-by-step construction of the Lewis structure of the carbonate ion

topics.title: Formal Charge
objectives: Student can calculate the formal charge on each atom in a Lewis structure
Student can use formal charges to choose the lowest-energy Lewis structure, as for ozone
visualIdeas: the ozone molecule with formal charges marked on each oxygen

topics.title: Limitations of the Octet Rule
objectives: Student can identify molecules with an incomplete octet (LiCl, BCl3), odd-electron molecules (NO, NO2) and expanded octets (PF5, SF6)
Student can state other drawbacks of the octet theory, such as not explaining shapes or relative stability
visualIdeas: Lewis structures of BCl3, NO and SF6 side by side

topics.title: Ionic or Electrovalent Bond
objectives: Student can relate the ease of forming an ionic bond to low ionization enthalpy and negative electron gain enthalpy
Student can define lattice enthalpy and explain how it stabilises ionic solids
visualIdeas: ions arranged in a sodium chloride crystal lattice

topics.title: Bond Length, Bond Angle and Bond Enthalpy
objectives: Student can define bond length using covalent radii and bond angle between orbitals around a central atom
Student can define bond enthalpy and explain average bond enthalpy for polyatomic molecules
visualIdeas: a water molecule with the O-H bond length and H-O-H angle marked

topics.title: Bond Order
objectives: Student can define bond order as the number of bonds between two atoms
Student can relate a higher bond order to greater bond enthalpy and shorter bond length
visualIdeas: H2, O2 and N2 with single, double and triple bonds

topics.title: Resonance Structures
objectives: Student can explain why one Lewis structure cannot describe molecules such as O3 and CO3 2-
Student can draw resonance structures and describe the resonance hybrid
visualIdeas: the canonical forms of ozone and their hybrid

topics.title: Polarity of Bonds
objectives: Student can explain polar covalent bonds and define dipole moment, and use it to explain the dipole moments of molecules such as H2O, BeF2, BF3, NH3 and NF3
Student can apply Fajans' rules to predict partial covalent character of ionic bonds
visualIdeas: bond dipole arrows in H2O, BeF2, NH3 and NF3

topics.title: The Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) Theory
objectives: Student can state the postulates of VSEPR theory and the order of repulsion lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair
Student can predict the shapes of molecules with only bond pairs, such as BeCl2, BF3, CH4, PCl5 and SF6
Student can predict the shapes of molecules with lone pairs, such as SO2, NH3, H2O, SF4, ClF3, BrF5 and XeF4
visualIdeas: ball-and-stick shapes from linear to octahedral
NH3 and H2O with lone pairs squeezing the bond angles

topics.title: Valence Bond Theory
objectives: Student can explain the formation of the H2 molecule from the attractive and repulsive forces as two H atoms approach
Student can relate the energy minimum on the potential energy curve to bond length and bond enthalpy, and describe bonding as orbital overlap
visualIdeas: a potential energy curve of two H atoms against internuclear distance

topics.title: Directional Properties of Bonds and Overlapping of Atomic Orbitals
objectives: Student can explain why simple overlap of atomic orbitals cannot explain the bond angles in CH4, NH3 and H2O
Student can distinguish positive, negative and zero overlap of atomic orbitals
visualIdeas: s and p orbitals overlapping in phase, out of phase and at right angles

topics.title: Types of Overlapping and Nature of Covalent Bonds
objectives: Student can distinguish sigma bonds formed by head-on overlap from pi bonds formed by sideways overlap
Student can explain why a sigma bond is stronger than a pi bond
visualIdeas: head-on s-s, s-p and p-p overlap beside sideways p-p overlap

topics.title: Hybridisation
objectives: Student can define hybridisation and state its salient features
Student can describe sp, sp2 and sp3 hybridisation with BeCl2, BCl3 and CH4
visualIdeas: an s orbital and three p orbitals mixing into four sp3 hybrids pointing to a tetrahedron

topics.title: Other Examples of sp3, sp2 and sp Hybridisation
objectives: Student can explain the shapes of NH3 and H2O using sp3 hybridisation with lone pairs
Student can explain the bonding in ethane, ethene and ethyne using sp3, sp2 and sp hybridisation
visualIdeas: ethene with sp2 sigma framework and sideways p overlap forming the pi bond

topics.title: Hybridisation of Elements involving d Orbitals
objectives: Student can describe sp3d and sp3d2 hybridisation in PCl5 and SF6
Student can explain why the axial bonds in PCl5 are longer than the equatorial bonds
visualIdeas: trigonal bipyramidal PCl5 and octahedral SF6

topics.title: Molecular Orbital Theory
objectives: Student can state the salient features of molecular orbital theory
Student can contrast molecular orbitals, which belong to the whole molecule, with atomic orbitals
visualIdeas: two atomic orbitals combining into a bonding and an antibonding molecular orbital

topics.title: Formation of Molecular Orbitals: Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals (LCAO)
objectives: Student can describe the formation of bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals by addition and subtraction of atomic wave functions
Student can explain why bonding orbitals have lower energy and antibonding orbitals higher energy
visualIdeas: constructive and destructive interference of two 1s orbitals

topics.title: Conditions for the Combination of Atomic Orbitals and Types of Molecular Orbitals
objectives: Student can state the conditions for atomic orbitals to combine: similar energy, same symmetry and maximum overlap
Student can distinguish sigma and pi molecular orbitals and their antibonding forms
visualIdeas: sigma and pi molecular orbitals formed from 2p orbitals

topics.title: Energy Level Diagram for Molecular Orbitals
objectives: Student can draw the molecular orbital energy level diagram for second period homonuclear diatomic molecules
Student can explain the different ordering of sigma2p and pi2p orbitals for O2 and F2 compared with B2, C2 and N2
visualIdeas: two MO energy diagrams side by side for N2 and O2

topics.title: Electronic Configuration and Molecular Behaviour
objectives: Student can relate the molecular orbital configuration to stability and calculate bond order
Student can predict bond length and magnetic nature (paramagnetic or diamagnetic) from the configuration
visualIdeas: MO boxes with unpaired electrons highlighted for O2

topics.title: Bonding in Some Homonuclear Diatomic Molecules
objectives: Student can write MO configurations for H2, He2, Li2, C2 and O2 and find their bond orders
Student can explain why He2 does not exist and why O2 is paramagnetic
visualIdeas: MO filling diagrams for H2, He2 and O2

topics.title: Hydrogen Bonding
objectives: Student can explain the cause of hydrogen bonding between a hydrogen atom and a highly electronegative atom such as F, O or N
Student can distinguish intermolecular and intramolecular hydrogen bonds with examples such as HF and o-nitrophenol
visualIdeas: zig-zag chains of HF molecules held by hydrogen bonds
o-nitrophenol with an intramolecular hydrogen bond

topics.title: The System and the Surroundings
objectives: Student can define the system, the surroundings and the boundary
Student can state that the system and surroundings together make up the universe
visualIdeas: a beaker of reacting solution as the system with the rest of the room as surroundings

topics.title: Types of the System
objectives: Student can distinguish open, closed and isolated systems by exchange of matter and energy
Student can give an example of each, such as reactants in an open beaker, a closed vessel and an insulated flask
visualIdeas: an open beaker, a closed flask and a thermos flask side by side

topics.title: The State of the System
objectives: Student can describe the state of a system by state variables such as pressure, volume, temperature and amount
Student can define a state function as a property that depends only on the state, not on how it was reached
visualIdeas: two different paths between the same initial and final states

topics.title: The Internal Energy as a State Function
objectives: Student can explain how internal energy changes by adiabatic work and by heat transfer
Student can state the first law of thermodynamics as delta U = q + w with the IUPAC sign convention
visualIdeas: a gas in an insulated container being stirred and a gas heated through a conducting wall

topics.title: Work
objectives: Student can derive the pressure-volume work w = -p_ex delta V for expansion against constant external pressure
Student can calculate work for isothermal reversible expansion of an ideal gas, w = -2.303 nRT log(Vf/Vi)
Student can explain free expansion and apply the first law to isothermal processes of an ideal gas
visualIdeas: a gas in a cylinder pushing a piston against external pressure
a p-V graph with the work shown as the shaded area

topics.title: Enthalpy, H
objectives: Student can define enthalpy H = U + pV and show that delta H equals the heat absorbed at constant pressure
Student can relate delta H and delta U for reactions involving gases using delta H = delta U + delta n_g RT
visualIdeas: heat flowing into a reaction at constant pressure with the system expanding

topics.title: Extensive and Intensive Properties
objectives: Student can distinguish extensive properties, which depend on the amount of matter, from intensive properties, which do not
Student can classify properties such as mass, volume, enthalpy, temperature and density
visualIdeas: a gas divided by a partition into two halves with each property compared

topics.title: Heat Capacity and the Relationship between Cp and CV
objectives: Student can define heat capacity, specific heat and molar heat capacity and use q = c m delta T
Student can derive Cp - CV = R for an ideal gas
visualIdeas: heating curves of samples with different heat capacities

topics.title: Measurement of ΔU and ΔH: Calorimetry
objectives: Student can describe the bomb calorimeter for measuring delta U at constant volume
Student can describe measuring delta H at constant pressure in a calorimeter and identify exothermic and endothermic reactions by the sign
visualIdeas: a cut-away bomb calorimeter immersed in water with a thermometer

topics.title: Standard Enthalpy of Reactions and Enthalpy Changes during Phase Transformations
objectives: Student can define reaction enthalpy and standard enthalpy of reaction, with the standard state of a substance
Student can use standard enthalpies of fusion, vaporisation and sublimation
visualIdeas: a table of enthalpies of fusion and vaporisation of common substances

topics.title: Standard Enthalpy of Formation
objectives: Student can define standard molar enthalpy of formation and state that it is zero for an element in its reference state
Student can calculate the reaction enthalpy from enthalpies of formation of products and reactants
visualIdeas: an enthalpy diagram with elements at zero and compounds above or below

topics.title: Thermochemical Equations and Hess's Law of Constant Heat Summation
objectives: Student can write a thermochemical equation with physical states and the enthalpy change
Student can state Hess's law and use it to calculate the enthalpy change of a reaction from other reactions
visualIdeas: two routes from reactants to products with enthalpy changes that add up to the same total

topics.title: Standard Enthalpy of Combustion and Enthalpy of Atomization
objectives: Student can define standard enthalpy of combustion and use it, for example for butane in cooking gas
Student can define enthalpy of atomization
visualIdeas: a gas stove flame burning butane

topics.title: Bond Enthalpy
objectives: Student can distinguish bond dissociation enthalpy for diatomic molecules from mean bond enthalpy in polyatomic molecules
Student can estimate the reaction enthalpy in the gas phase from bond enthalpies of bonds broken and formed
visualIdeas: bonds broken in reactants and bonds formed in products for the formation of HCl
